Main.lean.riemannHypothesis: Apply the reduction from right half-plane nonvanishing for Dirichlet L-functions to the Riemann Hypothesis. The nonvanishing theorem for every character supplies its hypothesis.
Main.lean.riemannZeta_eq_zero_re: Let s be a zero of the zeta function distinct from 1 and from the negative even integers. The Riemann Hypothesis established above applies to precisely these zeros and gives real part 1/2.
Main.lean.LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re: Fix a Dirichlet character and a point strictly to the right of the critical line. The assumption on the character or the point excludes the exceptional pair of the principal character and s = 1, so the right half-plane nonvanishing theorem applies.
Main.lean.LFunction_eq_zero_re: Fix a character and a zero in the open critical strip. The critical-strip conclusion of the combined nonvanishing theorem applies to all characters and forces real part 1/2.
Main.lean.LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive: Apply the critical-line theorem for primitive characters to the given zero in the open critical strip. It gives Re(s) = 1/2.

Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean.allChi: Apply the right half-plane nonvanishing theorem for every Dirichlet character to the given character and point.
Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean.rhOfAll: The reduction to the Riemann Hypothesis requires right half-plane nonvanishing for all characters. Apply it using the preceding nonvanishing theorem.
Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean.critAll: Fix a primitive character χ and a zero s with 0 < Re(s) < 1. Apply the primitive-character critical-line criterion with the right half-plane nonvanishing theorem. The criterion gives Re(s) = 1/2.
Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean.claimAll: Start with right half-plane nonvanishing for every character. The Dirichlet critical-strip reduction and the zeta-zero reduction give the other two conclusions from this same input. Combine the three claims.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.mem_span_of_C_pow_mul:
Write C(aᵛ)g = p C(aᵗ) + qXᵇ using membership in the two-generator ideal. For every degree n < b, the last term has coefficient zero. Comparing degree-n coefficients therefore gives aᵛgₙ = aᵗpₙ. Since a is nonzero and v ≤ t, cancel aᵛ to obtain gₙ = a^(t−v)pₙ.

Thus every coefficient of g − p C(a^(t−v)) below degree b vanishes. This difference is divisible by Xᵇ, so g is a linear combination of C(a^(t−v)) and Xᵇ.

Formalism/GammaFactorNonvanishing/CritLi.Formalism.VW.gammaFactor_ne_zero: For an even character the factor is Γℝ(s), and for an odd character it is Γℝ(s + 1). Both arguments have positive real part. The real gamma factor is nonzero in that half-plane.
Formalism/GammaFactorNonvanishing/CritLi.Formalism.VW.critLine:
A zero strictly to the right of the critical line contradicts the assumed nonvanishing at once. Suppose it lies strictly to the left. The gamma factor at s is nonzero, so the completed L-function also vanishes there. The inverse character is primitive because inversion preserves its conductor. Its functional equation now gives a zero of the completed L-function at 1 − s.

Dividing by the gamma factor transfers that zero to the ordinary L-function of the inverse character. The point 1 − s has real part greater than 1/2 and is distinct from 1, so this again contradicts the assumed nonvanishing. The remaining possibility is Re(s) = 1/2.
Formalism/GammaFactorNonvanishing/CritLi.Formalism.VW.rh_of_every: Take the trivial character of modulus 1, whose L-function equals the zeta function. The assumed nonvanishing for all characters therefore excludes zeta zeros with real part greater than 1/2 away from 1. The reduction for zeros of the zeta function now gives the Riemann Hypothesis.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.factor_ne_zero: The prime p exceeds 1, and Re(s) is positive, so the norm of p^(−s) is p^(−Re(s)) < 1. The norm of the character value is at most 1, hence the norm of their product is strictly below 1. The product cannot equal 1, which proves the Euler factor is nonzero.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.prim_zero: The change-of-level formula expresses the original L-value as the primitive L-value times a product of Euler factors. Here s is distinct from 1 because Re(s) < 1. Each Euler factor is nonzero since Re(s) > 0 makes the term subtracted from 1 have absolute value less than 1. The product can therefore vanish only through the primitive L-value.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.gamma_ne_zero: Distinguish even and odd characters. Their gamma factors are Γℝ(s) and Γℝ(s + 1), respectively. Positive real part of s implies positive real part of both arguments, so the factors are nonzero.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.prim_reflect: The gamma factor is nonzero at s, so the zero of the ordinary L-function gives a zero of the completed L-function. The inverse character is primitive by invariance of the conductor under inversion. Its functional equation transfers the completed zero to 1 − s. Since 1 − s is distinct from zero, the expression for the ordinary L-function in terms of the completed one gives the desired zero.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.strip: A zero above the critical line in real part contradicts right half-plane nonvanishing. For a zero below the critical line, first pass to the primitive character using the change-of-level formula. Its functional equation gives a zero at 1 − s for the inverse character. The reflected point has real part greater than 1/2 and is distinct from 1 because Re(s) > 0. This contradicts the same nonvanishing hypothesis, leaving Re(s) = 1/2.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.zeta:
A zero with real part at least 1 contradicts the usual zeta nonvanishing theorem. When the real part lies strictly between 0 and 1, view zeta as the L-function of the character of modulus 1 and apply the Dirichlet critical-strip result.

It remains to consider Re(s) ≤ 0. The value at zero is nonzero. The exclusions on s also ensure Γℝ(s) is nonzero, since its other zeros are the negative even integers. Thus the completed zeta function vanishes at s. Its functional equation transfers the zero to 1 − s, where the ordinary zeta function would then vanish with real part at least 1. This is impossible.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.zeta_iff: Both statements say that every zero of the zeta function other than 1 and the negative even integers has real part 1/2. Each direction follows by using the same hypothesis on those zeros.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_mem_vRing_iff: By definition, the valuation ring consists of the elements with nonnegative valuation. Applying this definition to x gives the equivalence.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_map_inv: The valuation of an inverse is the negative of the valuation of the original element. Applying this identity and substituting v(x) = n gives v(x⁻¹) = −n.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_isUnit_iff:
If x has an inverse y in the valuation ring, the valuations of x and y are nonnegative and sum to the valuation of 1, which is zero. Thus v(x) = 0.

Conversely, v(x) = 0 implies x ≠ 0 because the valuation of zero is the top element. The inverse has valuation −0 = 0 and belongs to the valuation ring. Together with the inverse identity in the field, this makes x a unit in the valuation ring.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_associated_pow: The equality v(π) = 1 implies π is nonzero and v(πⁿ) = n. Since v(x) = n as well, the ratio x/πⁿ has valuation zero. It belongs to the valuation ring and is a unit there. Multiplying πⁿ by this unit gives x, proving that the elements are associated.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_exists_nat: By discreteness the valuation of the nonzero element x is finite, so it is represented by an integer m. Membership in the valuation ring gives m ≥ 0. Take the natural number represented by m.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_irreducible: An element of valuation 1 is not a unit, since units have valuation zero. If π = ab, the two factors have nonnegative valuations whose sum is 1. Neither valuation can be the top element, and the remaining values are nonnegative integers. One of the two values is therefore zero. The corresponding factor is a unit, proving irreducibility.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_isDiscreteValuationRing: Choose π of valuation 1 using normalized discreteness. It lies in the valuation ring and is irreducible. Every nonzero element has a finite nonnegative integer valuation n and is associated to πⁿ. The criterion that a ring with such a uniformizer and factorization is a discrete valuation ring now applies.

Formalism/GammaFactorNonvanishing/RhOfRi.Formalism.VW.rh_of_right:
Let s be a nontrivial zero distinct from 1. The value of zeta at 0 also excludes s = 0. The assumed nonvanishing rules out Re(s) > 1/2. If Re(s) < 1/2, set t = 1 − s. Then Re(t) > 1/2 and t is distinct from 1, so ζ(t) is nonzero. The functional equation expresses ζ(s) as the product of ζ(t), Γ(t), cos(πt/2), and 2(2π)^(−t). The gamma and power factors are nonzero.

If the cosine vanished, t would equal 2k + 1 for an integer k, giving s = −2k. A negative k contradicts Re(s) < 1/2. The value k = 0 gives s = 0, and a positive k gives an excluded trivial zero. Thus the cosine factor is also nonzero. This contradicts ζ(s) = 0, so Re(s) = 1/2.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.FinalTheorems.everyCharacter: Use the Galois compatibility hypothesis to supply both compatibility entries of the literature hypotheses. The local reciprocity existence theorem supplies the remaining entry. The same Galois compatibility hypothesis gives the required window estimate. Apply the nonvanishing theorem with these literature hypotheses and that estimate.
The integral Galois compatibility theorem applied to the local reciprocity parameter gives the compatibility hypothesis of the preceding nonvanishing result. That result applies to every character.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.FinalTheorems.riemannHypothe: The preceding theorem supplies nonvanishing to the right of the critical line for all Dirichlet characters. The reduction from this nonvanishing statement gives the Riemann Hypothesis.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/ThetaC.UpperTheory.LiteratureTheorems.every_cha: Obtain the eigenvalue and first-stage results from the literature interface O. The same interface yields agreement of the theta integrals and local matching. Use the geometric and arithmetic results in O, together with the Hilbert–Samuel and bigness estimates, to obtain the covolume estimate. Supply these inputs, the local reciprocity existence theorem, and the window hypothesis to the nonvanishing result based on theta-integral agreement and local matching.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.Val.pow:
Unpack the normal-form data for a value of x. Each entry of the two characteristic vectors is either zero or one half, so both vectors coincide pointwise with their real-part vectors viewed over ℂ. The power formula for normal forms then gives the transformed data for y and its determinant relation.

Use the transformed data as the witnesses for the value of y. The new constant is cʲ and is nonzero because c is nonzero. Substituting the determinant relation and combining the powers gives the value tʲ.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.isElliptic_cube_sub: Compute the Weierstrass invariants of the model y² = x³ − x and substitute them in the discriminant formula. The discriminant is 64. It is nonzero, hence a unit in ℚ, which is the ellipticity criterion for the model.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.exists_known_rat:
Start with the rational elliptic curve y² = x³ − x. Its elliptic key has genus one and known value equal to the discriminant. Take its gth key power to get genus g. The proposed known value is the gth power of the discriminant.

After extension to ℂ, choose normal-form data for the original elliptic key. The discriminant formula gives its value in this normal form. The key power raises that value to the gth power by the formula for values of key powers. The base-change comparison and cancellation identify this normal form with the one for the given complex key of genus g, giving the required known value.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.zeta_ne_zero_of_everyCharact: Take the unique character modulo 1. Its L-function is the Riemann zeta function. Apply the assumed nonvanishing to this character and the given point s. The hypothesis s ≠ 1 supplies the required disjunction even for the principal character.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.riemannHypothesis_of_everyCh:
Let s be a nontrivial zero of the zeta function, with s ≠ 1. The right half-plane nonvanishing just proved rules out Re(s) > 1/2. Suppose Re(s) < 1/2. The value ζ(0) = −1/2 gives s ≠ 0. Then 1 − s is distinct from both 0 and 1, and Re(1 − s) > 1/2.

Write ζ(s) as the completed zeta function divided by Γℝ(s). A zero of Γℝ occurs only at 0 or a negative even integer, and both possibilities are excluded here. Hence the completed zeta function vanishes at s. Its functional equation gives the same zero at 1 − s. The quotient formula there gives ζ(1 − s) = 0, contradicting right half-plane nonvanishing. Thus Re(s) = 1/2.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.imprimitive:
Let ψ be the primitive character inducing χ. Primitive nonvanishing gives L(ψ,s) ≠ 0. If χ is nonprincipal, then ψ is nonprincipal, since changing the level of a principal character still gives a principal character. If s ≠ 1 this condition on the character is unnecessary. Thus the hypotheses allow the change-of-level formula for L(χ,s).

That formula multiplies L(ψ,s) by factors 1 − ψ(p)p^(−s). For each prime p in the product, |ψ(p)| ≤ 1 and |p^(−s)| = p^(−Re(s)) < 1, since p > 1 and Re(s) > 1/2. Hence ψ(p)p^(−s) cannot be 1. All factors in the formula are nonzero, so L(χ,s) is nonzero.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.plugWin: Take a witness of the family hypotheses. The Green condition supplies the shape theorem for these families, and applying it to the witness gives the connectedness criterion for the required families. For each primitive character ψ, the window input at ψ gives the required host existence by the host existence theorem for a character window. Apply the primitive-character nonvanishing theorem with these two inputs and window parameter 3/2, which exceeds 1.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.plugAll: First apply the preceding theorem to obtain the zero-free statement for primitive characters. Apply the imprimitive reduction to extend that statement to every Dirichlet character.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.hypV_of_cls: Take the eventual threshold x₁ + 1. At each x beyond this threshold and each index i, membership in the character family gives the two bounds at the corresponding host. The second is the required eventual volume bound.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.eFamC_of_cls: Use the constant 4 and the eventual threshold x₁ + 1. The character-family hypothesis supplies the cyclic-level estimate at the chosen host. Its scale coordinates are x and ε, by the two scale identities for the family. Substituting these coordinates gives the asserted eventual condition.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.zeroFreeAll_of_topG: Use the cyclic tied-window nonvanishing theorem with the given scaled families and their chain relation. Its comparison hypotheses are the level bound on family scales and the form-B theorem. For each ψ, apply the connectedness criterion using the host existence and eventual volume bound for the family class of ψ. This gives the exponents, a positive ε cutoff, and the required families. Each family supplies the eventual cyclic-level estimate by the preceding lemma, its windows directly from class membership, and the tie data from connectedness. The resulting nonvanishing theorem applies to every primitive character.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.supplyChi: Fix ψ and its window input. The admissible-host supply theorem reduces the conclusion to producing an admitted rank datum for each sufficiently large scale with the specified order and character-kernel conditions. For each ε in the required range, choose the threshold from the twisted-character admissibility theorem. After identifying the scale parameter with ε, the scale, order, and host assumptions are exactly those used by that theorem. Its rank datum supplies the admissible rank data required for host existence.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.hostOfField: Apply the host construction from field data. It takes the uniform short-norm estimates, including the estimate with norm bound one. With those inputs fixed, the construction supplies the constants and, for each admissible field datum in range, a host together with the required sharing estimate.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.supplyOfAdm: The general supply theorem converts admissible rank data and a character window into host existence. Use the preceding field-to-host construction. The resulting hosts satisfy both the cyclic-level estimate and the volume bound at the square root of the scale parameter.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.at_of_from: The From relation identifies the ranks of the point with R and identifies the transported host data with those of H. It also identifies the images of the two sets TT in the ambient frame coordinates. The frame coordinate map is injective, so equality of images gives equality of the sets themselves. After these identifications, the defining arguments of G.At at the point are exactly the arguments in the hypothesis on G.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.shapeWin:
Build the closed conditions for the design theorem from the given selections. The real-place tie, mass ratio, and genus mass inputs give the chosen-rank condition and the global link by the global-link theorem. To obtain the divisibility condition, first collect the restriction rows, stable cuts, chosen rows, one-map condition, nonnegative size, admissible twist link, and the two selection conditions. These conditions hold together by closure. For a family satisfying them, the wiring selection supplies the row maps when the required N-link is available. Use these maps and the collected conditions to form the bridge rows, then use the closed divisibility-link theorem.

For the existence input, intersect the original family class with the requested G-class. Restrict the selection and duty to this intersection. Forgetting the G-condition gives the original twisted and smoothed families, so the closed size and level conditions restrict as well. The design existence theorem now supplies designs in the intersection. Apply the design-window theorem with those designs, the closed divisibility condition just proved, and the eta, irreducibility, rank, G, S, and global links. The resulting connectedness is that of the requested G-class.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.topDesWin:
Combine the nine closed link conditions into one. Let ε₁ be its positive cutoff and ε₃ the positive cutoff for design existence. For 0 < ε < min(ε₁, ε₃), choose the threshold K given by the combined closed condition. Design existence above K produces a family in 𝒞′, together with its chosen data and size bounds. Map its class membership to 𝒞 to apply the closed conditions and to ℰ for the conclusion.

The ℰ membership gives the eventual volume bound. Use it with the N-link and the small-level rank equality to obtain divisibility in N. The closed divisibility condition, together with the eta and size inputs, then gives the required divisibility link. Combine this with the rank conditions and the two size estimates to obtain the μ-link. The global link now applies to the G, S, irreducibility, divisibility, and μ-links, producing the tied family required for connectedness.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.GlobalTheory.Fc.of_hyps: Apply the shape theorem to the family and selections carried by the hypothesis record. Pass the S-component of each C-selection. Translate the divisibility rows and the service condition using their equivalences in the shape interface. For the rank rows, retain the existing constants and eventual threshold, and keep the listed fields of the first row together with the second row intact. This gives the row condition in the form required by the shape theorem. The record and the supplied proofs of V and NR give all remaining inputs, so the theorem yields G.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.GlobalTheory.Fc.shape_of: Fix the four parameters and the shape theorem. Apply of_hyps with the supplied proofs of V and NR and the family hypothesis record to obtain G.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.mem_span_of_X_pow_mul:
Write X^ηg = F C(a) + G X^(b+η), where C(a) is the constant series a. If a = 0, the first term vanishes. Cancel X^η, which is nonzero in the power series domain, to obtain g = G X^b.

For a ≠ 0, rearrange to get F C(a) = X^η(g − G X^b). Its coefficients of degree below η vanish. Each is a times the corresponding coefficient of F, so that coefficient of F vanishes in the domain. Thus F = X^ηF′. Substitute this into the original equality and cancel X^η to obtain g = F′ C(a) + G X^b, which proves the desired ideal membership.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.pow_mem_span_pow_mul: Expand the yth power as u^y π₀^y q^((ℓ−1)y). Since M ≤ y and η ≤ (ℓ−1)y, factor π₀^M from the second factor and q^η from the third. The remaining factor is u^y π₀^(y−M) q^((ℓ−1)y−η). This exhibits membership in the ideal generated by π₀^M q^η.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.mem_cl: For the false orientation, membership in the window requires h−η ≤ u ≤ h−1. The strict inequality u < h−η excludes u from the window. Since u belongs to U, it belongs to the filtered complement for the false orientation.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.t3: The element u lies in the false-orientation complement by the preceding window comparison. Apply residue avoidance to u and k with the given lower and upper bounds on k. In this orientation the residue being tested is h−u.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.tele: Induct on the interval length k. At length zero the interval is empty and both sides equal M(a). For length k+1, add the endpoint a+k to the previous interval. The local relation at that endpoint gives f(a+k) + M(a+k+1) = g(a+k) + M(a+k), with arguments read modulo ℓ. Use this identity to move the new boundary term back to a+k, then apply the induction hypothesis to the old interval.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.q_numerical_identity:
Put d = ℓ−1 > 0. The natural-number quotient H′ / (ℓ−1) is at most H′/d in the reals. Combine it with the rational term in the bound on eW to get H′/d + H′ℓ/d² = H′(2ℓ−1)/d². This is at most H(2ℓ−1)/d² because H′ ≤ H.

If H is positive, H′+1 ≤ 2H, so log base ℓ of H′+1 is at most log base ℓ of 2H. If H = 0, then H′ = 0 and the logarithmic bound with the added 1 holds under Lean’s real logarithm convention. Substitute these bounds, cancel the +1 and −1 from the left side, and use the definition of aR.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.unit_coefficient_power_mod:
The definition of p₁ gives p₁ − uX^ℓ = C(ℓ)ε. Since a−b divides a^y−b^y, write p₁^y = (uX^ℓ)^y + C(ℓ)W for some series W. The coefficient of degree ℓy in (uX^ℓ)^y is the constant coefficient of u raised to y. Thus the coefficient of p₁^y has the required congruence modulo ℓ.

In the local-ring case, the constant coefficient of the unit u is a unit and remains one after taking the yth power. The correction term belongs to the maximal ideal because ℓ does. If the sum belonged to the maximal ideal, subtracting the correction would place that unit in the ideal, a contradiction. The coefficient is therefore a unit.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.truncation_remainder_bound:
Put A = π₀+ℓ. If y = 0, the assumed inequality forces c = 0, so 1 is already a generator. For y ≥ 1, reserve one factor π₀ and expand the remaining factor π₀^(y−1) as (A−ℓ)^(y−1). The term indexed by m contains π₀ A^(m+(ℓ−1)y) and (−ℓ)^(y−1−m), multiplied by a binomial coefficient.

If y−1−m ≥ c, this term is divisible by ℓ^c. Otherwise m ≥ y−c, so m+(ℓ−1)y ≥ ℓy−c ≥ K by the assumed inequality. In this case it is divisible by π₀ A^K. Every term is in the two-generator ideal, and so is their sum.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.truncation_signature_bound:
Put d = ℓ−1. For T ≥ 0, set A = ℓy−T. Multiplying the first general inequality by d reduces it to A ≤ d max(0,A), which holds because d ≥ 1. Thus ℓy/d − max(0,ℓy−T) ≤ T/d. Take T = X and T = η+M. Enlarging these right sides by the stipulated nonnegative amounts gives the first two bounds.

For the third bound set B = dy−X/ℓ. Multiplication by d² rewrites the left side as X + ℓB − d² max(0,B). If B ≤ 0, the correction is nonpositive. If B ≥ 0, it is (ℓ−d²)B, again nonpositive since ℓ ≥ 3. Divide by d² to get the stronger bound X/d², then add the allowed 1.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sum_erase_union_le: Removing zero from the union gives the union of the two sets with zero removed. The sum over this union plus the sum over the intersection equals the two separate sums. The intersection sum is nonnegative, so it can be dropped on the left.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sum_Icc_padicValNat_add_factorial_eq: At L = 0 the interval is empty. To increase L by one, add its new upper endpoint m+L+1 to the valuation sum. At the same time the factorial is multiplied by m+L+1. Valuations add under multiplication of these positive integers, so the induction identity is preserved.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sub_one_mul_padicValNat_factorial_le': Use the factorial valuation formula (ℓ−1)vℓ(N!) = N − sℓ(N), where sℓ is the base-ℓ digit sum. Its nonnegativity gives the desired bound.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.padicValNat_factorial_add_le_add_log: Factor (m+L)! as the product of m!, L!, and the binomial coefficient choosing L from m+L. These factors are positive, so their valuations add. The valuation of the binomial coefficient is at most the integer logarithm of m+L by the prime-factorization bound for binomial coefficients. Add this bound to the other two valuations.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sum_Icc_one_padicValNat_eq_factorial: Take m = 0 in the interval-factorial formula. The initial factorial is 0! = 1 with valuation zero, leaving the valuation of L! as the sum from 1 to L.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.first_sigma_valuation_bound:
Bound the sum on the union by the two interval sums with zero removed. On the first interval, reflect the negative integers and keep the positive ones. Valuation depends only on absolute value, so the two pieces are bounded by the factorial valuations at η−1 and η+a, using natural subtraction for η−1.

The second interval lies entirely below zero because b ≥ 2a+η+1. Reflection gives the interval from m+1 through m+a+S, where m = b−a−1. Its valuation sum is vℓ((m+a+S)!)−vℓ(m!). The binomial coefficient bound gives at most vℓ((a+S)!) + logℓ(m+a+S), with the integer logarithm in this expression.

Apply vℓ(N!) ≤ N/(ℓ−1) to the three factorial terms. Their numerator is at most 2a+2η+S. The integer logarithm is bounded by lam(ℓ,h+η), since m+a+S ≤ b+S ≤ h and the nonzero argument case follows by taking logs of ℓ^logℓ(N) ≤ N. For a zero argument the integer logarithm is zero. Finally lam(ℓ,h+η) is nonnegative, so increasing the logarithmic allowance to twice this quantity gives the stated bound.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.chain_len_add: Use the maps Y/X → Z/X → Z/Y induced by inclusion and quotient. The inclusion is injective because a representative from Y becomes zero exactly when it lies in X. The quotient map is surjective because the same representative in Z can be used in either quotient. Its kernel consists of classes represented by elements of Y, precisely the image of the inclusion. Length additivity for this short exact sequence gives the equality.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.chain_len_le_of_le_sup: Use the map from A/(A∩X) to Z/(Z∩X) induced by inclusion. Given a representative z in Z, write z = a+x with a in A and x in X, using Z ≤ A+X. The class of z is the image of the class of a. The map is surjective, so the target has length at most the source.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.chain_len_le_top: The map A/(A∩P) → M/P sends the class of a to its class in M/P. Every m in M can be written as a+p by the assumption M = A+P, so this map is surjective. Apply the length inequality for a surjection.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.comap_subtype_inf_of_le: An element of A already lies in C by the inclusion A ≤ C. Membership in B∩C on restricting to A is therefore equivalent to membership in B, giving equality of the two restricted submodules.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.column_chain_bound:
Induct on k. At k = 0 the sum is empty, and the terminal quotient represents the whole quotient since F₀ is the full module. For the induction step write U = Fₖ, V = Fₖ₊₁, X = P∩U, and Y = (V+P)∩U. Length additivity decomposes the old terminal term length(U/X) into length(Y/X) and length(U/Y). The latter is the new summand.

Since V ≤ U, the modular law gives Y = V+(P∩U). The map V/(V∩P) → Y/X is surjective by this equality, so length(Y/X) is bounded by the new terminal term. Substitute the two bounds into the induction hypothesis and append the new summand.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.len_coker_add:
The commutative squares induce maps A/a(A) → B/b(B) → C/c(C). The second map is surjective because g is. If f(x) = b(y), then c(g(y)) = g(f(x)) = 0. Injectivity of c gives g(y) = 0, so y = f(z) by exactness. Then f(x) = f(a(z)), and injectivity of f gives x = a(z). This proves injectivity of the first induced map.

If a class represented by y lies in the kernel of the second map, write g(y) = c(u) and lift u to v in B. Then g(y−b(v)) = 0. Exactness writes y−b(v) as f(z), so the class of y comes from A/a(A). Conversely g f = 0 makes every image class vanish. Length additivity on the resulting short exact sequence gives the formula.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sub_smul_one_injective: Take x in the kernel of q−ℓ·id. Then q(x) = ℓx, and linearity gives q^k(x) = ℓ^k x by induction. At k = n the nilpotence hypothesis gives ℓ^n x = 0. Since ℓ^n is nonzero and the module is torsion-free, x = 0.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.len_base: Choose a basis of R of cardinality r. In coordinates, the image of −ℓ·id is exactly the vectors whose entries are multiples of ℓ. Each such vector has a preimage by choosing a multiplier for every coordinate and negating it. The quotient is therefore the product of r copies of O/(ℓ). Add their lengths.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.len_main:
Induct on n. For n = 0, q = 0 and the formula for the zero operator applies. For the step, use the exact sequence ker q → R → im q, where the second map is q with its codomain restricted. The operator on the kernel is zero. The restriction to the image is killed by the preceding power, since every element of the image already has the form q(x). The three operators q−ℓ·id commute with the sequence, and the one on the image is injective by nilpotence and torsion-freeness.

Use additivity of cokernel length, then apply the induction hypothesis to the kernel and image, which are finite free submodules over the principal ideal domain. Their ranks add to the rank of R, by the quotient–image isomorphism and rank additivity. The two length formulas combine into the claimed one.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.length_pi_zero_bound: Choose an exponent n with q^n = 0. Then q^(n+1) is zero as well, so the nilpotent-operator length formula applies at n with the given scalar and yields the desired length formula.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.arc_exponential_identity: Because G ≥ 0 and j′ ≤ ell, we have j′G ≤ ell·G. If the maximum is 2σ+2j′G+1, bound it by 2σ+2ell·G+1 and add the prefactor. If the maximum is r+κ, the left side becomes 2r+4σ+2κ. The right side is larger by the nonnegative quantity 2σ+2ell·G+1.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sum_le_sum_cover: Each i in S belongs to at least one window, so its weight is bounded by the sum of its contributions over all windows. This uses nonnegativity of the weights. Sum over i, interchange the two finite sums, and collect precisely those elements of S lying in each window.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.kappa_window_bound:
The killer-polynomial valuation formula gives nonvanishing and expresses the valuation at 1 as ell plus the sum of 1+ell+vℓ(i) over the nonzero indices i. Let S be those indices. The windows cover S, so counting with weight 1 bounds its size by the sum of their lengths.

Apply the same covering inequality with weight vℓ(i). In each window, the selected indices are nonzero and satisfy |i| ≤ D. The window-sum estimate then gives Lₖ/(ℓ−1) + log base ℓ of D for their valuation sum. Sum the window bounds and add ell and the bound on the constant contribution (1+ell)|S|.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.second_exponent_bound: The proposed right side is nonnegative because ℓ ≥ 2 and all its terms are nonnegative. For the other entry of the maximum, cancel the two terms involving h″ and substitute the upper bound for c′. The terms involving b′ cancel. Now split (b+S+1)/(ℓ−1) into b/(ℓ−1) and (S+1)/(ℓ−1). The identity b/(ℓ−1) = b/(ℓ(ℓ−1)) + b/ℓ cancels the negative b/ℓ. Bound (S+1)/(ℓ−1) by S+1. The resulting bound is at most the claimed right side.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.length_quotient_le_of_pow_smul:
Let A be the sum of FFs and ℓ^(e′)M. Multiplying the first summand by ℓ^e puts it in J by hypothesis, and the second summand already lies in J and remains there after scaling. Thus ℓ^e annihilates A/(A∩J). The submodule generator bound controls its length by the rank of M times e times the length of O/(ℓ).

Use the sequence A/(A∩J) → M/J → M/(A+J). The first map is injective, and the second is a surjection. Its kernel consists of classes represented by a sum a+j, hence by a alone. This proves exactness and gives length additivity. Finally M/(A+J) is a quotient of M/A and has at most its length. Combine the two bounds.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.log_nat_le: At h = 0 the real logarithm is zero by convention. For h > 0, split log h as log(h/1000) + log 1000. Apply log t ≤ t−1 to both terms and add the bounds.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.mpar_le: The integer quotient in Mpar is bounded by the real quotient (h+2g)/(ℓ−1). Since ℓ−1 ≥ 10 and the numerator is nonnegative, replace the denominator by 10. Adding 1 gives the claim.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sig_lt: The power ℓ^(j−1) is at least 1, so the Mpar term after division by that power is bounded by Mpar itself. For ℓ ≥ 11, the bound ℓ/(ℓ−1)² ≤ 11/100 follows after clearing denominators from (ℓ−11)(11ℓ−1) ≥ 0. Substitute the bound on Mpar, then use that the ceiling of a nonnegative real is strictly less than that real plus 1. The 1 already in the argument of the ceiling makes the total rounding allowance 2.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.rr_le: For the two rational terms use ℓ ≥ 11 and (ℓ−1)^(j+1) ≥ 10². Since log ℓ ≥ 1 and log h ≥ 0 for natural h under the real logarithm convention, log base ℓ of h is at most log h. Use the upper bound for the logarithm of a natural number and substitute the three bounds into the assumption on rr.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.exists_constant_exponent_inequalities:
Take C = 100000. Put G = w+S+η and z = G+1, so b ≥ 100000(j+1)z ≥ 200000z. This gives max(G,1) < b ≤ min(b₀,b₁) and η < b. Hence b₀ ≤ b+η < 2b ≤ 2b₁, which gives both comparisons with ℓb₁ because ℓ ≥ 11.

For the final bound use g = max(G,1) ≤ z and H = b+η+S ≤ b+G in the preceding bounds for the two exponents. The definition a₀ = 2σ + rr + 2g·ell and ell ≤ 3j+1 then with σ denoting the sigma exponent give a₀ < 0.242b + (6j+20000)z by collecting the coefficients. For j ≥ 1, 6j+20000 ≤ 11000(j+1), so the second term is at most 0.11b. Thus a₀ < b/2 ≤ b₁/2.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.lam_ge_one: If H = 0, log base ℓ of 2H is zero by the real logarithm convention. If H is positive, then 2H ≥ 1, so this logarithm is nonnegative since ℓ > 1. In either case adding 1 gives at least 1.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.hcoef_le: Bound the three terms by (41/2)/x², 10/x², and (11/10)/x², respectively. For the first two, clear the positive denominators and put t = x−11 ≥ 0. The differences become (9/2)t³+95t²+518t+172 and 2t²+24t+32. For the third, the cleared inequality is 10x ≤ 11(x−1). Adding the three bounds gives 31.6/x² ≤ 32/x².
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.expBound_statement:
Put H = h+η, d = ℓ−1, and L = lam(ℓ,H). Insert the upper bounds on s₁, e₂, and both occurrences of E. Bound b by H and the integer quotient in sig by h/d ≤ H/d. The terms involving a now sum to 8a/d. By the assumption on a and the definition of aR, this contributes at most 8H(2ℓ−1)/d³ + (32+8L)/d.

Collect the H terms to obtain H·[8(2ℓ−1)/d³ + 8/d² + 1/(ℓd)]. The coefficient bound gives at most 32H/ℓ². The remaining terms are 10η/d, (3+3/d)S, and 9L+10+(34+8L)/d. Since d ≥ 10, the S coefficient is at most 4. Since L ≥ 1, the last group is at most 24L. These are the required terms.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.hCoef_num: Put t = x−11 ≥ 0. The polynomial expands to 7t³+153t²+920t+892. Every term is nonnegative.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.h_coefficient_bound: Subtract the three terms on the left from 32/x² and use the common denominator x²(x−1)³. The numerator is 7x³−78x²+95x−32, which is nonnegative by the preceding numerator estimate. The denominator is positive for x ≥ 11, so the difference is nonnegative.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sigma_exponent_le_real: Write d = ℓ−1 and m = j−1. Use Mpar ≤ (h+2g)/d + 1, the floor bound on the integer quotient. In the argument of the ceiling, the contribution from 3g is at most 9g/4 because ℓ/d² ≤ 3/4. The remaining Mpar contribution is bounded by the sum of (h+2g)ℓ/(d³ℓ^m) and (ℓ/d²)/ℓ^m. For the first use ℓ ≤ 3d/2 and d^m ≤ ℓ^m. For the second use ℓ^m ≥ 1 and ℓ/d² ≤ 3/4. Finally allow the existing 1 and up to 1 more for the ceiling. This yields the stated constant 11/4.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.total_exponent_le_eight_hundred:
Put T = h/(ℓ−1)^(j+1), U = g·ell, and L = log base ℓ of h. Unfold the total exponent to obtain 4rr+8σ+4U+2kap. Since G/ℓ ≤ g/3, the rr bound is 20(g/3+T+L+1). Using (ℓ−1)^(j+1) ≥ 4 in the sigma estimate gives the sigma exponent σ ≤ 3T/2+3g+11/4. For kap, use 4g/(ℓ−1) ≤ 2g and log base ℓ of 2h ≤ L+1.

Substitution gives coefficients 92 for T and 90 for L. All remaining terms are bounded by 269U, using g ≤ U, ell ≤ U, and 1 ≤ U. Since T, U, and L are nonnegative, the resulting sum is at most 800(T+U+L).

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.eta_determinant_comparison: Apply the determinant comparison input with the supplied ring action and element Θ. Its remaining premise is the product congruence for an arbitrary tuple of elements of R′ and a test point. View each tuple entry as a matrix-valued function over the fraction field. The hypothesis on R′ gives the action compatibility for each of these functions, so the product congruence input applies and supplies the premise.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.iter_nzd: Induct on n. For n = 0 the hypothesis is already the desired membership. In the successor case write ℓ^(n+1)z as ℓ(ℓ^n z). The one-factor saturation condition gives ℓ^n z in the ideal, and the induction hypothesis gives z in the ideal.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.saturation_criterion: Identify A with its image in its fraction field. Choose b = f′x in A and a in A with fa = ℓ^k x. Multiplication by f′ gives ℓ^k b = f′fa in the fraction field and hence in A. Saturation of (f′), applied k times, gives b = f′c for some c in A. Cancel the nonzero f′ in the field to obtain x = c. Now ℓ^k c = fa in A. Apply saturation of (f) k times to obtain c = fd, as required.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.submodule_generator_count:
First bound the length of O/(ℓ^n) by n times the length of O/(ℓ). At n = 0 the quotient is zero. For the induction step the natural map O/(ℓ^(n+1)) → O/(ℓ^n) is onto. Its kernel is a quotient of O/(ℓ), via multiplication by ℓ^n, since each representative in the kernel is a multiple of ℓ^n. Length additivity gives the bound at n+1.

Now put Q = F∩P. Over the principal ideal domain, F has a finite basis of size k at most the rank of M. The classes of its basis elements generate F/Q, and the assumption says ℓ^e kills every class. Sending one standard generator to each basis class therefore gives a surjection from k copies of O/(ℓ^e) onto F/Q. Add the lengths of these copies, apply the bound at n = e, and replace k by the rank of M.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.exists_sep: For each pair y ≠ x choose a function f in T with f(y) ≠ f(x). Subtract the constant function f(x). This factor vanishes at x and is nonzero at y. For fixed y, multiply these factors over all x ≠ y, using 1 at x = y. The result eᵧ lies in T and has support exactly {y}, since O is a domain. Sum the eᵧ over y outside S. At any point of S all terms vanish, and at a point outside S exactly its own term survives.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.disj: Choose the separating function u for S and let g be its action on V. By the definition of Vₓ, g acts on it by the image of u(x) in the fraction field. For x in S this eigenvalue is zero. For x outside S it is nonzero, since the field embedding is injective. Thus VS for S lies in the zero eigenspace, and VS for the complement lies in the sum of the nonzero eigenspaces. Independence of eigenspaces at distinct eigenvalues makes these two spaces disjoint.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.geom_sum_range_mul_one_sub: Use induction on n. The empty sum yields zero on both sides. Increasing n by one adds x^n(1−x) to the product. Combining it with the inductive value 1−x^n gives 1−x^(n+1).
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.tsum_le_two_level: The nonnegative sequence is summable by its geometric majorant. Split the sum before index j. The first j terms contribute at most (A+D)(1−x^j)/(1−x). The tail contributes at most (B+D)x^j/(1−x), by shifting the index and summing the geometric series. Adding gives (A+Bx^j+D−Ax^j)/(1−x). Drop the nonnegative subtracted term Ax^j/(1−x).
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.rr_arith: Insert the bound on s and the value q = d/(d−1) into the estimate for r. This gives r ≤ (2G+2hy+C+3)F+C, where F = (d+1)/(d(d−1)). For d ≥ 2, clearing positive denominators shows F ≤ 10/(d+1), F ≤ 3/d, and F ≤ 3/2. For the 10/(d+1) and 3/2 bounds, the differences are 11+(d−2)(9d+6) and (d−2)(3d+1)/2, respectively. The 3/d bound reduces to d+1 ≤ 3(d−1). Apply these bounds to the G, hy, and C+3 terms, respectively. Then C ≤ 3+L bounds (C+3)·3/2+C by 12+5L/2 ≤ 20(L+1).
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.remainder_bound_of_tsum: Let d = ℓ−1, x = 1/d, L = log base ℓ of h, and C be the ceiling of 1+log base ℓ of 2h+1. Since h ≥ 1, we have 2h+1 ≤ 3h and log base ℓ of 3 ≤ 1. The ceiling bound gives C ≤ 3+L. Apply the two-level geometric estimate with initial coefficient 2G, tail coefficient 2h, and common offset C+3. This gives s ≤ (2G+2hx^j+C+3)/(1−x). Apply rr_arith with y = x^j and q = 1/(1−x) = d/(d−1). Its term hy/d equals h/d^(j+1), giving the desired remainder bound.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.comap_subtype_span_sup_eq_span_range_sup: Write A for the ambient span of s, which lies in Z. After mapping the two submodules into the ambient module via the inclusion of Z, the left side is (A+J) ∩ Z. The internal generators map to exactly the elements of s, so the right side maps to A+(J∩Z). These images agree by the modular law, since A ≤ Z. Injectivity of the inclusion gives equality of the submodules in Z.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.length_quotient_le_of_two_step:
Inside Z/(I∩Z), let N be the image of the span of s₀. The restriction identity for spans shows that N is generated by the classes of s₀. They are killed by ℓ^e′, so the length of N is at most g₀e′ times the length of O/(ℓ). Indeed, a module generated by g₀ such classes is a quotient of g₀ copies of O/(ℓ^e′), and each copy has length at most e′ times the length of O/(ℓ).

The quotient by N is Z modulo the restriction of span(s₀)+I. The classes of s generate this quotient because span(s)+I = Z, and these classes are killed by ℓ^e. The same estimate gives the bound with ge. Add both estimates along the exact sequence for N.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.len_two_step: Include B/(B∩P) into A/(A∩P) and then quotient A by A∩(B+P). The inclusion is injective because an element of B represents zero in A/(A∩P) exactly when it is in P. The second map is onto. Its kernel consists of classes of a = b+p, with b in B and p in P. These are precisely the image of the first map, since a and b have the same class. Add lengths in the resulting short exact sequence.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.len_chain: At k = 0 the initial term is the quotient M/P, since F₀ is the full module. In the induction step apply the two-step length equality to Fₖ₊₁ ≤ Fₖ. It rewrites the old terminal length as the next layer length plus the next terminal length. Insert that equality into the bound for k and append the new summand.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.len_bound: Since Bc is contained in I, its image is zero in Z/(Z∩I). The equality Z = span(s)+Bc then says the classes of s generate the quotient. They are killed by a^e, and therefore give a surjection from |s| copies of O/(a^e). Each copy has length at most e times the length of O/(a). Use |s| ≤ g to finish.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sub_gen: Take a basis of F over the principal ideal domain and view its vectors in M. They form a finite spanning set of size at most the rank of F, which is at most the rank of M. Apply the quotient length bound for a finite spanning set with Bc = 0, I = P, and g equal to the rank of M, using the hypothesis that a^e kills the classes of F modulo P.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.column_assembly_bound: Use the chain length inequality to bound the length by the sum of layer lengths and the terminal length. For i in gen, the chosen generators and Fᵢ₊₁ span Fᵢ, so the quotient length bound for a finite spanning set applies with Bc = Fᵢ₊₁ and I = Fᵢ₊₁+P. This gives coefficient me′ in units of the length of O/(ℓ). For each other i, the assumed bound gives coefficient L. There are |gen| indices of the first kind and k−|gen| of the second because gen is contained in the index range. Add the layer estimates. Finally the bound for a submodule generated by a basis gives coefficient rank(M)·e for the terminal length. Factoring out the common length proves the formula.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.ramified_valuation_inequality:
Write ℓ as a unit times ϖ^e, where e > 0. Thus ℓ is a nonunit. For each i between 0 and y, write the binomial coefficient choosing i from y as ℓ^vᵢ times a positive integer prime to ℓ. The latter is a unit in O. Indeed, its Bézout relation with ℓ expresses 1 as a sum of two terms, and the term divisible by ℓ is a nonunit. In the local ring the other term must be a unit.

Expand p₁^y by the binomial theorem. Its ith summand is a unit series times X^(ℓi) times the constant series ϖ^(e(vᵢ+y−i)). The series is a unit because it is a product of the prime-to-ℓ factor, powers of the given units, and a power of the unit relating ℓ to ϖ^e. The X-exponents are distinct. The ideal-membership criterion for such a sum says that each term either has X-exponent at least b or has ϖ-exponent at least t.

Set i₀ = floor((b−1)/ℓ). Then ℓi₀ < b ≤ ℓ(i₀+1) and b ≤ ℓy, so i₀ < y. The criterion gives t/e ≤ vᵢ₀+y−i₀. The binomial coefficient valuation is at most the integer logarithm of y to base ℓ, which in turn is at most the real logarithm. Also i₀ ≥ b/ℓ−1. Substituting gives the claimed bound with room to spare.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sum_shift_val: The map j ↦ j₀−j is injective, so replacing the indices by their images preserves the sum. The weight of each image index i is vℓ(i).
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.g_coeff_valuation_statement:
Split S₂ at b. Combine its portion above b with the indices in [b−a+1,b] other than j₀, since these two sets are disjoint. The other portion of S₂ lies in [1−η,η+a]. Reindex both sums injectively by i = j₀−j. The first image lies in the half-open interval starting at j₀−b−S−a of length 2a+S. The second lies in the interval starting at j₀−η−a of length 2η+a. Neither contains zero, since j₀ was removed from the central interval and the two ranges for S₂ lie outside it. The bounds on b and S also give |i| ≤ 2(h+η) in both images.

Apply the valuation window estimate to both images and sum. The length contribution is (3a+S+2η)/(ℓ−1). The logarithmic contribution is twice log base ℓ of 2(h+η), which is at most 3 lam(ℓ,h+η) by the definition of lam and nonnegativity of that logarithm.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.winDiff: Reindex by the injective map j ↦ j₀−j. The image lies in the half-open window starting at lo with length L. Zero is absent because j₀ is absent from T, and the absolute values are bounded by D. Apply the valuation window estimate to this image.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.g_ideal_valuation_statement:
Let S₁ = [b−a+1,b]. The hypothesis b ≥ 2a+η+1 puts S₁ strictly above the low interval for S₂, and the other interval for S₂ starts at b+1. Thus the two sets are disjoint. The Lagrange ideal lifting theorem supplies ideal membership at exponent E, the supremum over j₀ in S₁ of the valuation sum on S₂ and on S₁ with j₀ removed. Its association hypothesis is exactly the one assumed for the differences of c.

For a fixed j₀, split the sum into S₁ with j₀ removed and the high and low portions of S₂. Their differences j₀−j lie in windows of lengths a, S+a, and 2η+a, respectively. All differences are nonzero by disjointness and the removal of j₀. The interval endpoints and b+S ≤ h give |j₀−j| ≤ h+η. Apply the window valuation estimate to each of the three parts. The lengths add to 3a+S+2η, and each logarithm is at most lam(ℓ,h+η). This bounds every value in the supremum and hence E. If S₁ is empty, E is zero and the bound follows by nonnegativity.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.chain_of_step: Take the chain of length one with cuts a and b. Its only step is the supplied step from a to b.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.chain_trans: Concatenate the cut sequences, identifying the last cut of the first chain with the first cut of the second chain at b. Use the first chain's indices through its endpoint and subtract its length from each later index. Each adjacent pair lies in one of the original chains, including the pair that starts at b. Hence every pair is a valid step, and the endpoints are a and d.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.fill:
Use strong induction on the length s of the initial empty interval. If s < 2j, go directly from a to e. The length is at least j and at most s+j+1 ≤ 3j. The first j places are empty, and every marked point up to e lies after a+s. There are at most two such points by the tail assumption, so the direct step is valid.

If s ≥ 2j, first take a step of length j through the empty interval. From a+j, the remaining empty interval has length s−j ≥ j and still ends at a+s, so the tail assumptions are unchanged. The induction hypothesis gives a chain for this shorter interval. Concatenate the initial step and that chain.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.pair:
At the marked point g, the cluster condition must take its second form because f is a marked predecessor within distance j. The unique permitted predecessor in the stated range is therefore f itself. All points strictly between f and g are excluded.

If there were a marked point h in (g,g+j], apply the same condition at h. The permitted predecessor would have to be g, at distance h−g. But f would be a second marked predecessor at distance (h−g)+(g−f), which is at most (h−g)+j. This violates the exclusion range at h. Hence the whole interval (g,g+j] is empty.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.cluster_chain:
Induct on a natural bound for the distance B−a. Let f be the first marked point after a, which exists at or before B. The empty starting interval forces f > a+j. Set s = f−1−a. If the j places after f are empty, take e = f. Otherwise choose a marked g within that window and take e = g. The pair lemma gives an empty j-window after g and excludes marks strictly between f and g. Also g ≤ B, since otherwise B would either lie strictly between f and g or, if B = f, have a marked point in its own empty window.

In either case the tail (a+s,e] contains at most two marks, namely f and possibly g, and has length at most j+1. Apply fill to reach e. If e = B this is the desired chain. Otherwise e has an empty starting window and B−e is strictly smaller than B−a. Apply induction and concatenate.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.main:
If there are no marked points, take a = 0 and use fill on the empty interval of length n, with no tail. Otherwise start with a marked point t₀. If the next j places are empty, take t = t₀. If there is a mark g among them, take t = g, whose next j places are empty by the pair lemma.

Periodicity makes B = t+n a marked point and transfers the empty window after t to the window after B. Since n ≥ j+1 and j ≥ 1, the cut-chain lemma applies from t to B with distance bound n. This gives a chain spanning one period.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.C_mem_polyS: The constant polynomial C(c) has coefficient c in degree zero and zero in all higher degrees. Both values lie in S.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.X_mem_polyS: The coefficient of X in degree one is 1, and all its other coefficients are zero. The subring S contains both values.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.comp_mem_polyS: Expand p(q) as the finite sum of C(pₑ)qᵉ over the degrees in p. Each constant C(pₑ) belongs to the coefficient subring, and every power of q does too. Closure under products and finite sums gives the result.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.term_newL: Write L₀ = (c₀,d₀,g₀) and L = (c,d,g). The new triple has scalar c₀ᵏc, degree kd₀+d, and monoid element g₀ᵏg. Multiplicativity of the representation and of the constant-polynomial map gives the matrix factor ρ(g₀)ᵏρ(g), with entries mapped into R[X]. Multiplying the scalar monomials gives C(c₀ᵏc)X^(kd₀+d). This is the product of the kth power of the term for L₀ with the term for L, in that order.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.F_perm: Permuting the triples permutes the list of their matrix terms. Its sum is unchanged by commutativity of matrix addition, so taking the determinant of the identity minus that sum gives the same polynomial.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.charpoly_comp: The reversed characteristic polynomial of ρ(g) is the determinant of I−Xρ(g), with the matrix entries regarded as constants. Substitute C(c)Xᵈ for X in this determinant for L = (c,d,g). Substitution fixes scalar entries and commutes with determinants. The resulting matrix is I minus the term attached to L.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.piN_eq_zero: Since d ≥ N+1, the monomial C(c)Xᵈ is divisible by X^(N+1). It therefore vanishes in the quotient by that principal ideal.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.mapMatrix_smul_zero: The entry in position (i,j) of the mapped matrix is the product of the images of a and Mᵢⱼ. The first factor is zero, so every entry vanishes.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.geom_list: For N = 0 both sides equal 1−x. At the next step the finite sum acquires x^(N+1). Left multiplication by 1−x adds x^(N+1)−x^(N+2) to the previous value 1−x^(N+1). This gives the required value at N+1. The calculation uses only powers of the same element and works in a noncommutative ring.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.alg_identity: Let P = 1+x+⋯+xᴺ and Y be the sum of the list ys. For each power of x, distribute left multiplication over the sum Y. The total sum inside the second factor is then PY. The finite geometric identity and x^(N+1) = 0 give (1−x)P = 1. Hence (1−x)(1−PY) = (1−x)−Y = 1−(x+Y). The products keep x and its powers on the left throughout.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sum_flat: Induct on the outer list. The empty list gives zero. For a head a followed by a tail, the flattened list is h(a) appended to the flattened tail. Its sum after applying f splits accordingly, and the induction hypothesis identifies the second sum.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.key:
Work in the coefficient ring modulo X^(N+1). Let x be the matrix term of L₀ there. The positive X-degree of L₀ makes x^(N+1) zero. For each term y from the rest of the list, the new triples represent the products xy through xᴺy by the formula for the new matrix terms. Thus the eliminated list sums to (1+x+⋯+xᴺ)Y, where Y is the original sum of the rest.

Apply the algebraic identity to factor I−(x+Y) as (I−x) times the identity minus the new sum. The quotient map commutes with determinants, and the determinant of a matrix product is the product of determinants over the commutative coefficient ring. This gives the asserted factorization in the quotient.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.base: In the quotient modulo X^(N+1), every scalar monomial in the list is zero because its degree is at least N+1. Thus the sum of matrix terms vanishes. The image of F is the determinant of the identity, which is 1.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.letter_mem: By the substitution formula, the single-letter determinant is the reversed characteristic polynomial of ρ(g) evaluated at C(c)Xᵈ. The characteristic coefficients lie in S by hypothesis, and the substituted monomial has its coefficients in S because c belongs to S. Composition preserves this coefficient condition. Passing to the quotient gives membership in the image subring.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.stepD:
Induct on the number of letters of degree exactly D. With no such letters, all degrees are at least D+1 and the given higher-degree result applies. Otherwise move one degree-D letter to the front and factor it out by the determinant factorization. Its single-letter factor belongs to the image subring by the single-letter coefficient result.

In the remaining list, the old letters retain their coefficients and degrees. Each new letter multiplies an old coefficient by a positive power of the removed one, so the coefficient remains in S. Its degree is the old degree plus a positive multiple of D and is strictly larger than D. Thus the number of degree-D letters drops by exactly one, and the induction hypothesis puts the remaining determinant in the image subring. Multiply the two factors there.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.allD: Induct on the amount j by which the lower degree bound can be raised before it reaches N+1. If j = 0, all terms vanish in the truncation and the determinant equals 1. For the successor step, increasing the minimum degree from D to D+1 makes the induction hypothesis available. The degree-elimination lemma transfers that result back to lists of minimum degree D.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.core: Truncate at degree k. The degree-elimination result with initial degree bound 1 puts the class of F in the image of the polynomials over S. Choose a polynomial q over S representing that class. The difference F−q is divisible by X^(k+1), so its coefficient in degree k is zero. Thus the degree-k coefficient of F is the corresponding coefficient of q and belongs to S.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.mem_mainNotions_iff_fromT: The carrier of the subalgebra is defined to consist of the functions from T. Membership therefore says exactly that the function comes from T.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.S1_mem_OmF: The carrier of S1 requires each multivariate coefficient function to lie in the subalgebra of functions from T. Unfolding that carrier replaces each such membership by the assertion that the coefficient function comes from T, which is the right-hand side.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.charpolyRev_map: Apply the coefficient ring homomorphism to the determinant that defines the reversed characteristic polynomial. It commutes with determinants, fixes the polynomial variable, and maps the constant matrix entries through f. Entry by entry the result is the defining matrix for the reversed characteristic polynomial of M with entries mapped through f.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.det_eq_coeff: In a subsingleton ring the two values agree. Otherwise let d be the matrix dimension. The characteristic polynomial has degree d, so reversing it makes its constant coefficient the degree-d coefficient of the reversed polynomial. The constant coefficient of the characteristic polynomial is (−1)ᵈ det M. Multiplication by (−1)ᵈ gives the asserted formula because its square is 1.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.F_eq: Every letter has degree one. For L = (c,1,g) its term is X times the constant-coefficient matrix obtained from cρ(g). Summing these identities factors out X, and the constant-coefficient map commutes with the matrix sum. This also holds for the empty list, whose sums vanish.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.det_poly_statement:
For each matrix aᵢ choose its finite representation as a sum of group matrices with coefficient functions from T. Multiply each coefficient function by the multivariate variable Xᵢ. The resulting polynomial-valued function belongs to S1 because its only possibly nonzero coefficient is the original function. Lift the group matrices to matrices of constant multivariate polynomials, retaining their dependence on the test point. Evaluation at a point commutes with the reversed characteristic polynomial, so its only possibly nonzero multivariate coefficient comes from the original characteristic coefficient function. The input hypothesis puts that function in T.

Use these weighted group matrices as the letters of the determinant argument, all with degree one in the auxiliary polynomial variable. The core result puts the coefficient in degree d, the matrix dimension, into S1. Since the letters all have degree one, their determinant polynomial is the reversed characteristic polynomial of the summed weighted matrix. The sign formula converts that coefficient to the determinant, still in S1.

At each test point, expand the finite sum and use the chosen representations of the aᵢ. The weighted matrix evaluates to the sum of Xᵢaᵢ with entries mapped to constant multivariate polynomials. Evaluation commutes with the determinant. Taking the requested multivariate coefficient now gives a function from T by the defining condition of S1.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.X_pow_mul_C_mem_coneAlg: Let W be the range of ev. Induct on the construction of t as an element of Wᵈ. In degree zero, a ground scalar gives a constant polynomial, which lies in the algebra. Addition of elements of Wᵈ corresponds to addition of their degree-d monomials. In the multiplication step write the new coefficient as ev(v)t′, with t′ in the preceding power. Its monomial is the product of X·C(ev(v)) and the monomial for t′. The first factor is a generator of the cone algebra and the second belongs by induction.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.mem_coneAlg_iff_coeff:
Write W for the range of ev. For the forward direction, the condition that the coefficient of degree d belongs to Wᵈ is preserved by the operations generating the algebra. The generator X·C(ev(v)) has its only possibly nonzero coefficient in degree one, where it lies in W. Ground scalars contribute only in degree zero, where W⁰ is the ground-scalar submodule. The condition is closed under addition degree by degree. In a product, each contribution to degree d is a product of coefficients from degrees i and j with i+j=d, so it belongs to WⁱWʲ = Wᵈ. The sum of these contributions also belongs.

Conversely, expand p as the finite sum of its coefficient monomials. The preceding lemma puts each monomial Xᵈ·C(p_d) in the algebra because p_d belongs to Wᵈ. Closure under finite addition gives p in the cone algebra.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.rootOfUnity_mem_range_Om: Choose a primitive mth root ζ in Om ℓ. The embedding into ℂ_[ℓ] is injective, so the image of ζ is still primitive of order m. Its m powers from exponent 0 through m−1 are distinct roots of X^m−1. Since that polynomial has degree m, these exhaust its roots. In particular x is one of those powers. The same power of ζ in Om ℓ maps to x because the embedding preserves powers.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.finsum_fiberwise_of_finite_support:
Let S be the finite support of f. For each b, the sum of f on the fibre ρ⁻¹(b) is the finite sum over those a in S with ρ(a) = b. To see this, extend the summand on the fibre by zero to all of A. The extension is supported in S, and the terms outside the fibre vanish.

If b lies outside ρ(S), the fibre sum is zero. The outer sum can therefore be taken over the finite image ρ(S). The fibres over this image partition S, so adding their sums gives the sum of f over S, which is the original finitely supported sum.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.coercive_of_re_pos:
Write q(x) = Re Q(x,x). If V has only the zero vector, q(0) = 0 by bilinearity and c = 1 suffices. Suppose V has a nonzero vector. Linear maps from a finite-dimensional normed space are continuous, so Q can be viewed as a continuous linear map into the space of continuous linear maps V → ℂ. Evaluating on the diagonal and taking the real part gives a continuous function q.

The unit sphere is nonempty and compact, so q has a minimum c there. Every unit vector is nonzero, hence the positivity hypothesis gives c > 0. For x ≠ 0, set u = x/‖x‖. Then u has norm one, and bilinearity gives q(x) = ‖x‖² q(u) ≥ ‖x‖² c. At x = 0 both sides vanish.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.localization_away_injective_of_dvd:
Let I be the kernel of R → R_𝔭 and choose a finite generating set for I using Noetherianity. Each generator maps to zero in R_𝔭, so some element outside 𝔭 annihilates it. Take t to be the product of these elements, using 1 for the empty set. The complement of 𝔭 is multiplicatively closed, so t is outside 𝔭. It annihilates each generator and therefore all of I.

Write c = td and fix a compatible map κ from R[1/c] to R_𝔭. The images of t and d multiply to the unit image of c, so the image of t is a unit in R[1/c]. If a fraction a/cⁿ belongs to the kernel of κ, multiplying its image by the image of cⁿ shows that a maps to zero in R_𝔭. Hence a lies in I and ta = 0. Since t maps to a unit in R[1/c], a maps to zero there as well. The fraction is zero and κ is injective.

Development/AutomorphicSpectrum/Proofs/B.liftSemi_tmul: Through the algebra map R → S, the target is an R-module and the semilinear map f becomes R-linear. The base-change lift extends this map to the tensor product. The extension is S-linear and sends 1 ⊗ x to f(x), so it sends s ⊗ x = s · (1 ⊗ x) to s · f(x).

Development/AutomorphicSpectrum/Proofs/B.liftSemi_piS_bijective: For the finite index set I, tensoring with S over R identifies the tensor product of S with ∏ᵢ Mᵢ with the product ∏ᵢ (S ⊗ Mᵢ). Under this identification the lifted product map is the product of the individual lifted maps. Indeed, on a pure tensor s ⊗ x its i-th component is s · uᵢ(xᵢ) on both sides. The maps are additive, so the identity holds on all tensors. Each component lift is bijective by hypothesis, and their product composed with the tensor-product identification is bijective.
Development/AutomorphicSpectrum/Proofs/B.liftSemi_cT_bijective: The base-change data at T provides an S-linear equivalence e sending 1 ⊗ b to the image of b under the component map at T. By S-linearity e sends s ⊗ b to s times that image. This is also the value of the objectwise lift on s ⊗ b by the pure tensor formula. The lifts agree on pure tensors and extend additively, so the objectwise lift equals e and is bijective.
Development/AutomorphicSpectrum/Proofs/B.comparison_degree_zero_bijective: A degree-zero cochain has one component for each object T. The comparison map is the lift of the product of the component maps at these objects. Each objectwise lift is bijective by the objectwise bijectivity lemma. Apply the finite-product lemma to the object index.
Development/AutomorphicSpectrum/Proofs/B.comparison_degree_one_bijective: A degree-one cochain is indexed by pairs of objects T, T′ and arrows T → T′. On the component for an arrow the semilinear comparison acts by the component map at T′. Its lift is bijective by the objectwise bijectivity lemma. Apply the finite-product lemma to the arrows for each fixed pair, then to T′ for each T, and finally to T.
Development/AutomorphicSpectrum/Proofs/B.comparison_degree_two_bijective: A degree-two cochain is indexed by triples of objects T, T′, T″ and composable arrows T → T′ → T″. The component map is the map at the final object T″, whose lift is bijective. Combine these lifts with the finite-product lemma, first over the second arrow, then over the first arrow, and then over T″, T′, and T in that order.
Development/AutomorphicSpectrum/Proofs/B.th_bijective: The opposite of the finite poset P has finitely many objects. Each hom-set in its category has at most one element because an arrow is specified by a single order relation. The degree-zero, degree-one, and degree-two comparison lemmas now apply to the given base-change data. Together they prove the three bijectivity assertions.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.restrictIdeal_eq_comap_ι: The restriction of I to U is defined by pulling back I along the open immersion U → X. This is exactly the ideal on the right.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.restrictIdeal_eq_top_iff_forall_notMem_s: An ideal sheaf is the unit ideal exactly when its support is empty. The support of the pullback to U is the inverse image of the support of I under U → X. A point of U is a point x of X with x ∈ U, and it belongs to that inverse image exactly when x belongs to the support of I. Thus the restricted ideal is the unit ideal exactly when every point of U avoids the support of I.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.restrictIdeal_eq_comap_homOfLE_restrictI: The inclusion V → X is the composite V → U → X. Pullback along this composite first restricts I to U and then pulls that restricted ideal back to V. This is also the direct restriction of I to V.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.restrictIdeal_eq_of_le_of_eq: Express the two restrictions to V as pullbacks along V → U. Their inputs are the equal restrictions of I and J to U, so the pullbacks agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.restrictIdeal_comap_eq_comap_resLE_restr: Since f sends V into U, the two composites V → X → Y and V → U → Y agree, with V → U the restriction of f. Pullback of I along the first composite restricts the pullback along f. Pullback along the second composite pulls back the restriction of I to U. Functoriality identifies the two ideals.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.zeroLocus_eq_support: The zero locus of an ideal sheaf is defined to be its support as a closed subset of X.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.vanishesAlong_iff_le: Vanishing of I along J is defined to mean that I is contained in J. Both directions are the identity on this condition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.nonzeroOnComponents_iff: The definition requires each irreducible component to have a point outside the support of I. This is precisely the stated condition that no component is contained in that support.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isSmoothDivisor_iff: The definition imposes two conditions. The ideal D is locally generated by a non-zero-divisor, and the subscheme cut out by D is smooth over the base via its inclusion followed by p. These are the two conditions on the right.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coordSubspaceIdeal_eq_ofIdealTop_span_co: Take the coordinate functions indexed by S in the coordinate ring of the affine space. The coordinate subspace ideal sheaf is defined by taking the sheaf associated to the ring ideal they generate, giving the displayed formula.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.EtaleChart.coordIdeal_eq_comap_coordSubs: The chart ideal for S is defined by pulling back the coordinate subspace ideal for S along the chart's étale map.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.inStrictNormalCrossingPosition_iff: By definition, the global condition consists of smoothness of each divisor in E and the local chart condition at every point of X. Unfolding it gives exactly the stated conjunction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.hasStrictNormalCrossingsWith_iff: Unfold the condition at a point x of the support of Z. It asks for an étale coordinate chart around x and an assignment of optional coordinate indices to the entries of E. An unassigned entry restricts to the unit ideal, and an assigned entry restricts to the corresponding coordinate hyperplane ideal. Distinct assigned entries use distinct coordinates. In the same chart, Z restricts to the ideal of the coordinates indexed by S. These are exactly the witnesses and conditions on the right.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.HasStrictNormalCrossingsWith.exists_etal: Apply the defining local condition of h at the given point x of the support of Z. This supplies the chart, the assignment for E, and the coordinate set for Z with all the required properties.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.hasStrictNormalCrossingsWith_of_forall_e: For each x in the support of Z, the hypothesis supplies a chart with distinct coordinate indices for the assigned entries of E and the required coordinate ideal for Z. These pointwise data give the defining condition for strict normal crossings along Z.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.inStrictNormalCrossingPositionAt_of_exis: Use the given neighbourhood, chart, and assignment in the definition at x. The three conditions in the hypothesis say that assigned indices are distinct and determine the restrictions of every assigned or unassigned entry of E.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.InStrictNormalCrossingPositionAt.exists_: Unfold the local condition at x. Its witnesses are the neighbourhood, chart, and coordinate assignment, and its three requirements give exactly the desired properties.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.HasStrictNormalCrossingsWith.exists_etal:
At x, choose the local chart, the coordinate set S for Z, and the assignment b for the full list H :: E. Keep the chart and S. Assign b(0) to H and b(i+1) to the i-th entry of E. The old ideal conditions at index 0 give the two possibilities for H. At index i+1 they give the two possibilities for the corresponding tail entry.

If a tail entry uses the coordinate assigned to H, injectivity on the assigned coordinates gives i+1 = 0, which is impossible. If two tail entries use the same coordinate, injectivity gives i+1 = j+1 and hence i = j. The original ideal condition for Z applies to the retained chart and S.

Formalism/LocalToGlobal/GroupLattices/Ti.FullTiedNoG.toFull_base: Completing the datum copies the underlying tied data from X and adds g. Its base projection is therefore the original base of X.
Formalism/LocalToGlobal/GroupLattices/Ti.FullTiedNoG.toFull_g: Completing the datum sets the G-data to g. The G-data are therefore the supplied g.
Formalism/LocalToGlobal/GroupLattices/Ti.hermitian_setting_level_zero: The change of datum copies the tied Hermitian fields from H. In particular, its level-zero Hermitian data are those of H.
Formalism/LocalToGlobal/GroupLattices/Ti.adSet: The change of datum replaces the assigned G-data and its dimension certificate. The adjacency conditions use the original lattice and step data, the Hermitian columns, and the data at T. The change of datum copies the Hermitian columns and the data at T field by field. Consequently the upward, downward, and dilation conditions at level zero and at positive levels are identical to the six supplied conditions in h. Use those six fields for the new adjacency structure.
Formalism/LocalToGlobal/GroupLattices/Ti.full_setting_level_zero: The adjusted tied datum is built by applying the Hermitian change of datum to the original base. That change copies the level-zero field, so the completed datum has the original level-zero data.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_subschemeMap_isOpenImmersion: The closed subscheme defined by the pulled-back ideal on V is the fibre product of V and the closed subscheme defined by D over W. Take its projection to the latter closed subscheme. That projection is the base change of the open immersion V → W, so it is an open immersion. The fibre product square gives the required equality of composites.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isOpenImmersion_subschemeMap: The fibre product construction supplies an open immersion with the required composite into W. Any other map with the same composite agrees with it because the closed immersion into W is a monomorphism. The given map is therefore an open immersion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isSmoothDivisor_comap: Restricting to an open subscheme preserves the local description by one non-zero-divisor. The pulled-back closed subscheme maps to the original divisor by an open immersion, which is smooth. Composing it with the original divisor's smooth map to the base field gives the smooth structure map of the pulled-back divisor.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.inStrictNormalCrossingPositionAt_nil: Smoothness supplies an étale chart on an open neighbourhood of x. Use the assignment that selects no coordinate at any index. The empty list has no valid indices, so the distinctness and both ideal conditions hold vacuously.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.inStrictNormalCrossingPosition_nil: There are no divisors in the list to check for smoothness. At each point the preceding local result supplies the required étale chart for the empty list.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.filterNeTop_nil: Filtering only retains entries of the original list. The empty list has none, so the filtered list is empty.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.filterNeTop_cons_of_ne_top: The first ideal passes the test for being different from the unit ideal. It is retained as the first entry, followed by the filtered tail.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.filterNeTop_cons_top: The first ideal is the unit ideal and fails the filter. The result is the filtered tail.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_of_mem_filterNeTop: Every occurrence retained by the filter comes from an occurrence in the original list, giving the asserted membership.
